The tool is neutral by default; the profile table shows how values match works.

Method

Each choice is shown side by side, with no scores. Records (what candidates did) come first, then questionnaire answers, then other statements, then donors and endorsements. Every line shows its kind, topic, date and source. After each comparison, a table shows how six example values profiles would score it from the same evidence; those scores are illustrations, not recommendations.

U.S. Representative, District 6 (2-year term)

Emily Randall (Prefers Democratic Party)

  • [Taxes and budget] RECORD, 2025-07-03: H.R. 1 (the 2025 budget reconciliation act) final passage, roll call 190, July 3, 2025: passed 218-214. Randall voted No. (source: clerk.house.gov)
  • [Sports eligibility] RECORD, 2025-01-14: H.R. 28 (Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act) passage, roll call 12, January 14, 2025: passed 218-206, 1 present. Randall voted No. (source: clerk.house.gov)

  • [Federal funding] STATED, 2026: In her voters' pamphlet statement she reports securing nearly $18 million in federal funding for community projects across the district's six counties. (source: www.sos.wa.gov)
  • [Campaign finance] FUNDER, 2026-07-15: FEC 2026 cycle through 2026-07-15: $1,195,246.70 raised, of which $876,066.66 from individuals and $311,706.07 from other committees; $981,487.55 spent; $241,630.83 cash on hand. (source: www.fec.gov)

Teresa Fox (Prefers Republican Party)

  • [Economy and natural resources] STATED, 2026: In her voters' pamphlet statement she lists maritime industries, timber, naval strength and technology jobs as priorities and favors balanced budgets and 'science-based stewardship' of forests. (source: www.sos.wa.gov)
  • [Campaign finance] FUNDER, 2026-07-15: FEC 2026 cycle through 2026-07-15: $27,615.02 raised; $24,778.90 spent; $2,836.12 cash on hand; $12,343.78 debts; includes $7,515.00 in candidate loans. (source: www.fec.gov)

Initiative Measure IP26-645 (taxes on individual income)

IP26-645 would repeal the 9.9% tax on annual individual income over $1,000,000 enacted in 2026 and prohibit state and local taxes on individual income.

What YES does:

  • A yes vote repeals the 9.9% tax on individual income over $1,000,000 before it begins in 2028 and prohibits taxes measured by individual income (Attorney General explanatory statement, https://www.sos.wa.gov/sites/default/files/2026-10/Voters%20Pamphlet%202026%20-%20Edition%2009%20-%20Pierce.pdf).

What NO means: A no vote leaves the 2026 law (ESSB 6346) in place, so the 9.9% tax on individual income over $1,000,000 begins in calendar year 2028 (Attorney General explanatory statement, https://www.sos.wa.gov/sites/default/files/2026-10/Voters%20Pamphlet%202026%20-%20Edition%2009%20-%20Pierce.pdf).

Cost estimate: The Office of Financial Management estimates a state revenue loss of $11,432,414,000 over fiscal years 2027-2031, mainly from the general fund, with no impact on local revenue (https://www.sos.wa.gov/sites/default/files/2026-10/Voters%20Pamphlet%202026%20-%20Edition%2009%20-%20Pierce.pdf).

Strongest argument for YES: Argument for, written by Chris Gildon and others: Washingtonians have rejected an income tax ten times, and the measure 'restores your right to decide'. (www.sos.wa.gov)

Strongest argument for NO: Argument against, written by the Washington Education Association, Washington State Labor Council and others: the measure cuts billions for education and healthcare and benefits those earning over $1 million. (www.sos.wa.gov)

  • [Taxes] STATED, 2026: Official ballot title (voters' pamphlet): "Initiative Measure No. IP26-645 concerns state and local taxes. This measure would repeal a 9.9% tax on annual individual income over $1,000,000; prohibit taxes measured by individual income and taxes on individual income or the receipt of individual income; and define “income.” This measure would decrease funding for public K-12 education, higher education (including universities and community colleges), and human services (primarily healthcare). Should this measure be enacted into law?" (source: www.sos.wa.gov)
  • [State budget] STATED, 2026: Office of Financial Management fiscal impact statement: estimated state revenue loss of $11,432,414,000 over state fiscal years 2027-2031; $3.108 billion in FY2029, $4.432 billion in FY2030, $3.892 billion in FY2031. (source: www.sos.wa.gov)
  • [Arguments] STATED, 2026: The pamphlet printed an argument for (Gildon and others) and an argument against (Washington Education Association, Washington State Labor Council and others), each with a rebuttal; the argument against names one YES-side funder. (source: www.sos.wa.gov)
  • [Campaign finance (YES)] FUNDER, 2026: PDC: Vote Yes Repeal the Income Tax reports $1,586,970.00 in contributions and $269,085.14 in expenditures; Let's Go Washington (Sponsored by Brian Heywood), registered for IL26-001, IL26-638 and IL26-645, reports $3,876,110.50 in contributions and $3,613,312.13 in expenditures across all three measures. (source: www.pdc.wa.gov)
  • [Campaign finance (NO)] FUNDER, 2026: PDC: No on 645 reports $11,522,533.97 in contributions and $429,686.81 in expenditures; Millionaire's Tax Washington (against) reports $243,799.00 in contributions and $219,039.23 in expenditures. (source: www.pdc.wa.gov)

What to check: Whether the revenue the tax would raise is worth more to you than the measure's broader ban on income taxes, given the state's $11.4 billion revenue-loss estimate over fiscal years 2027-2031.

Open items

  • Pierce County Council district for the test address (Tacoma is split across districts) and whether that district is up in 2026; the county council seats on the 2026 ballot are Districts 1, 5 and 7 per an aggregator (The Ballot Brief), not confirmed from the county.
  • Pierce County Superior Court judge races, Pierce County District Court positions (an aggregator and PDC data disagree on Position 5 candidates), and Tacoma Municipal Court contests: PDC lists three Tacoma Municipal Court candidates but contested status is unconfirmed.
  • Pierce County charter amendments (a Pierce County page reportedly lists seven on the Nov 3, 2026 ballot) and any City of Tacoma measures or other local districts (school, fire, port): the county Elections site and local voters' pamphlet returned 403 to automated access and could not be opened.
  • Congressional and legislative districts came from the U.S. Census Bureau geocoder (CD 6, LD 27 as of its current boundary layers), not the VoteWA address lookup.
  • Pierce County Auditor candidate list rests on PDC data and an aggregator; the official county sample ballot could not be opened.
  • Pierce County Prosecuting Attorney candidate list (Coreen E. Schnepf, Bryan Chushcoff): from PDC registrations only (both shown on the general ballot); not confirmed on the county sample ballot.
  • Pierce County Auditor: PDC also lists Mitchel (Mitch) Townsend as a 2026 County Auditor candidate shown on the general ballot; not reconciled with the two names listed here.
  • Local voters' pamphlet and sample ballot from piercecountywa.gov were blocked (HTTP 403 / Cloudflare check), so county and city items are incomplete; the state/federal list comes from the official Washington voters' pamphlet (Pierce edition).
  • No local measure was researched because none could be confirmed from an official source; only one measure (IP26-645) was researched, so 4 items instead of 5.
  • Prosecutor race: no voted or decided records found for either candidate from sources I could open; both candidates' items are campaign-site statements and PDC totals. No League of Women Voters or Vote411 questionnaire was found.
  • Teresa Fox and Carole Sue Braaten have no legislative record; Braaten has no PDC totals.
  • FEC figures run through 2026-07-15 (latest report in the FEC API when checked); PDC figures are the 2026 campaign summary dataset at the time checked.
  • Measure funding is committee-level; top donors were not listed.
